newsitem.title: GERMANY: German farmers consider offers for malting barley.
newsitem.headline: German farmers consider offers for malting barley.

text.p: Lower consumer price ideas for malting barley from the 1997 harvest have created problems for German farmers assessing pre-fixed contract offers, industry sources said.
"The price is down because ample supply from the 1996 crop is still around and maltsters and brewers expect only steady beer sales this year," a grains analyst said.
"Farmers may accept lower prices, or risk losing more money if there is another record crop ... alternatively they may move into other grains or oilseeds for spring plantings."
The malting barley market relies on pre-harvest contracts because weather patterns are crucial to the supply of malting quality. Great risks are involved on both sides.
Malting barley carries a premium over feed barley but farmers get no premium for selling surpluses into intervention.
Bids for ex-farm purchases in classic growing regions amount to 290-300 marks a tonne in Lower Saxony, 285-292.50 marks in Bavaria and around 300 marks in Rhineland Palatinate.
Lower Saxony farmers must decide on the contracts by February 28, after which prices are expected to drift lower.
Last year, some 320-340 marks were offered and 60 percent of the crop was fixed before changes in the weather generated a bumper crop, which weighed down prices of unfixed material.
Of the 4.2 million tonnes of spring barley harvested (up from 2.9 million in 1995), around 57 percent qualified for malting, according to broker estimates.
"Consumers now have an extra two months' worth of cover from the 1996 crop," said a source at the Lower Saxony chamber of agriculture.

Domestic consumption of malting barley of around 1.9 million tonnes should not shift much because beer output and exports would be merely stable after a decline last year, said an official at the brewers association, Brauerbund, in Bonn.
He said the spring barley area should be unchanged or lower than the estimated 793,000 hectares sown last year.
With a lower land set-aside rate, farmers had planted four percent more 1996/97 winter grains.
Unlike last year, there would be little additional spring grain area from replantings because of limited winter damage.
German beer output in 1997 should be little changed from 114 million hectolitres in 1996, which was down 2.2 percent on the previous year.
